sections.h2: What a Kansas transfer on death deed is
sections.html:
A transfer on death deed, also called a TOD deed or beneficiary deed, names the person who will receive a piece of real estate when the owner dies. Until then the owner keeps full control. It looks like a regular deed but does not take effect until death. The rules sit in Article 35 of Chapter 59 of the Kansas Statutes, K.S.A. 59-3501 and following.

The roles are simple. The owner is the grantor, the person who will receive the property is the grantee beneficiary, and the deed stays revocable for the owner's whole life. It covers land and homes, and it can also cover certain oil, gas and mineral rights and royalties.

The deed has to be signed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, and all of that must happen before the owner dies. K.S.A. 59-3502 supplies the wording: the owner transfers on death to the named beneficiary, followed by the description of the interest. The deed must also say that it is revocable and transfers no ownership until the owner's death. The abbreviation "TOD" may replace the full words.

  • Copy the legal description from your current deed, so get a copy of that deed first.
  • Sign before a notary. Johnson County and Wyandotte County both turn away deeds with incomplete notary certificates.
  • Record it before death. Johnson County's filing rules require a TOD deed to be filed before the grantor dies.
  • Skip the beneficiary's signature. The statute makes the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice unnecessary.

Wyandotte County posts sample forms, including a general TOD deed and a joint tenancy version. Registers cannot draft documents for you. Ask a lawyer or title company when the facts are not straightforward.

sections.h2: What happens when the owner dies
sections.html:
Title passes to the named beneficiary at the moment of the owner's death, and that property needs no probate. Under K.S.A. 59-3504, title to real estate recorded in TOD form vests in the designated grantee beneficiary on the death of the record owner.

The beneficiary takes the house with everything the owner had attached to it. The statute lists conveyances, contracts, mortgages, liens and security pledges, plus any executory contract of sale, option to purchase, lease, easement or deed of trust. It also names claims of the State of Kansas for medical assistance. A TOD deed does not wipe the slate clean.

How a TOD deed works over time
Point in timeWhat the law provides
While the owner is alive (K.S.A. 59-3502, 59-3503)Deed transfers no ownership; owner can sell, revoke or change it
At the owner's death (59-3504(a))Title vests in the grantee beneficiary
After vesting (59-3504(b))Beneficiary takes subject to liens, mortgages, leases and Medicaid claims
If the beneficiary dies first (59-3504(c))Transfer lapses unless an alternate or surviving issue qualifies

The beneficiary usually records a certified death certificate so the public record shows why title moved. The Johnson and Wyandotte registers both take a state-certified copy under K.S.A. 58-501 and 65-2416, with no alterations or attachments.

sections.h2: Revoking or changing a TOD deed
sections.html:
Any time before death, you can revoke or change a Kansas TOD deed by recording a new instrument. Under K.S.A. 59-3503 a revocation must be executed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds where the land is, and the beneficiary's consent or notice is not needed. A later TOD deed automatically revokes all earlier beneficiary designations for the same interest.

One rule catches people out: a recorded TOD deed may not be revoked by a will. Simply denying a TOD in a will does not undo it. The Wyandotte register records revocations of TOD deeds and asks for the book and page number of the deed being revoked.

sections.h2: If the beneficiary dies before the owner
sections.html:
The gift lapses unless the deed names an alternate or the 2023 rule for surviving descendants applies. Under K.S.A. 59-3504(c), if a grantee beneficiary dies first and no alternate is named, the transfer to that beneficiary lapses. There is an exception. When the deed was not made contingent on the beneficiary surviving the owner and the beneficiary leaves at least one surviving child or other issue, the interest vests in those descendants per stirpes.

That exception comes from a 2023 amendment and applies to deeds filed of record on or after July 1, 2023 (K.S.A. 59-3504(e)). Older deeds follow the older rule. A court action to decide who succeeds goes through the probate code's descent procedure. A frequent mistake is naming one beneficiary and never planning for that person dying first.

A TOD deed skips probate for the house and keeps the owner in control, but it does not shield the property from debts or taxes.

  • Probate is avoided for the property, even if the same person is named in the will.
  • The beneficiary's own creditors cannot reach the property while the owner is alive, since the beneficiary has no interest yet.
  • It does not avoid the owner's creditors or state estate recovery.
  • It does not cause a Medicaid transfer penalty, since ownership does not move until death.
  • It does not replace a will. The rest of the estate still needs a plan.

It also costs far less than a probate. A transfer through a TOD deed is much cheaper than a transfer under a will or revocable trust, because it avoids court and clerical fees.

sections.h2: Selling a house that has a TOD deed
sections.html:
While the owner is alive, the owner can sell, because the deed gives the beneficiary no ownership. You still own your property and can sell it at any time. A sale by the owner is an ordinary deed transfer with the usual sales validation questionnaire and recording steps, which our Kansas quitclaim deed guide covers.

After the owner dies, the beneficiary holds title and can sell, subject to the existing mortgage and liens. Because the house passed outside probate, the beneficiary usually does not need a court appointment to sell it. Other assets in the estate may still be going through the court, so see our page on the Kansas probate process if the estate is open.

Beneficiaries who inherit a house they do not want to keep, or one that needs repairs, can ask us about an as-is cash sale. The title company will look at the recorded TOD deed, the death certificate and any open liens, so gather those first.

sections.h2: Titling a vehicle in TOD form
sections.html: K.S.A. 59-3508 allows a motor vehicle to be titled in TOD form by naming a beneficiary on the certificate of title. This is handled through the county treasurer or tag office, usually at registration time, and must be done for each vehicle. It is a separate process from the real estate deed recorded with the register of deeds.

Pull your current deed and confirm exactly how title is held. Decide on a beneficiary and an alternate. Have the new deed prepared, signed before a notary and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the property sits. Keep a copy of the recorded deed with your other papers, and tell the person who will handle your estate where it is.

faqs.q: Is a TOD deed legal in Kansas?
faqs.a: Yes. Kansas authorizes transfer on death deeds in K.S.A. 59-3501 and following. The deed must be signed, acknowledged and recorded with the register of deeds in the county where the land lies before the owner dies.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to sign a Kansas TOD deed?
faqs.a: No. K.S.A. 59-3501 and 59-3503 say the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice is not required while the owner is alive. The deed also needs no consideration.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house after recording a TOD deed?
faqs.a: Yes. The deed transfers nothing until your death, so you can sell the property, revoke the deed or change the beneficiary during your life.

faqs.q: Does a TOD deed avoid probate in Kansas?
faqs.a: It avoids probate for the property it covers. The beneficiary takes the house subject to liens, mortgages and state medical assistance claims, and the rest of the estate may still need probate.

faqs.q: What if my TOD beneficiary dies first?
faqs.a: The transfer lapses unless an alternate beneficiary is named. For deeds filed on or after July 1, 2023, surviving children or other issue of the beneficiary can take instead, unless the deed was made contingent on the beneficiary surviving the owner.
